title: Secrets and the software supply chain
summary: Keep secrets out of code, issue short-lived scoped credentials from a vault or workload identity, rotate and revoke fast, pin and verify dependencies, and harden CI because it holds the keys to production.
principle: Assume every secret will leak eventually and every dependency could be compromised, then limit the blast radius. **Secrets**: never in code or images; fetched at runtime by an identity, scoped to least privilege, short-lived, rotated automatically and revocable in minutes. **Supply chain**: know what you ship (lockfiles, SBOM), install exactly what you reviewed (pinning, hashes), verify where artifacts came from (signatures, provenance), and treat CI as production infrastructure because it can deploy to production.
why:
Leaked credentials are one of the most common ways into a system, and they leak through boring paths: a key committed to git (deleting the file leaves it in history), a `.env` in a container image, a token printed in a CI log, a laptop backup. Automated scanners watch public repositories, so a pushed key can be abused within minutes.

**Secrets management.** Store secrets in a vault or the cloud provider's secret manager, encrypted with keys in a KMS. Workloads authenticate with an identity they already have (a cloud instance or pod role, a CI job's OIDC token) and receive secrets or, better, **short-lived credentials** at runtime, so there is no long-lived secret to steal in the first place. Scope each credential to one service and the actions it needs. Rotate on a schedule and immediately on suspicion; design for two valid versions during the overlap so rotation is not an outage.

**Dependency risk.** Most of your code is other people's. Risks include known-vulnerable versions, typosquatted names, **dependency confusion** (an internal package name published publicly with a higher version), maintainers' accounts being hijacked, and install scripts that run code on your build machine. Controls: commit a lockfile and install with it (`npm ci`, `pip install --require-hashes`), pin CI actions and base images by digest, pull through an internal mirror or a scoped registry, generate an **SBOM** (SPDX or CycloneDX) so you can answer "are we affected?" in minutes, and patch on a schedule.

**Provenance.** Signing proves who published an artifact; provenance describes how and from what it was built. **SLSA** is a framework of levels for build integrity, roughly from "provenance exists" up to "provenance is generated by a hardened, isolated build platform". **Sigstore** tooling (for example `cosign`) can sign artifacts with short-lived certificates tied to an OIDC identity and record signatures in a public transparency log. These raise the bar; they do not prove the code itself is safe.

**CI hardening.** CI has write access to your registry and often your cloud. Give jobs read-only tokens by default, use OIDC federation instead of stored cloud keys, keep secrets away from jobs that run untrusted pull-request code, require review and branch protection, and use ephemeral runners.

diagrams.title: The lifecycle of a secret
diagrams.alt: State flow of a secret. It is generated by the vault, stored encrypted, granted to a specific workload identity, and used at runtime. Every access is written to an audit log. On a schedule or on suspicion it is rotated, which stores a new version, and the old version is revoked after an overlap window.
diagrams.caption: The healthy loop has no human copying values around. If rotation is a manual, scary event, it will not happen when you need it.

steps.text: The vault generates the value (or the provider issues it), so no human ever types or sees it, and it never passes through chat, email or a ticket.
Access is granted to a workload identity, not to a person or a shared account, and only for the paths it needs: `orders-api` may read `prod/orders/db`, nothing else.

The service fetches the secret at startup or on demand and keeps it in memory, never in an image, a config file in git or an environment dump in logs. Each read is audit-logged so you can scope an incident.
Rotation runs on a schedule and on any alarm. The new version is stored while the old one is still valid, so running instances can pick it up without downtime.
After the overlap window the old version is revoked. If you only ever rotate during incidents, you will discover at the worst time that nobody knows which services use the key.

diagrams.title: Hard-coded key vs fetched short-lived token
diagrams.alt: Side-by-side comparison. On the left, a cloud key is written in source code, lands in git history and from there leaks through a fork, a log or a laptop, and stays valid for months. On the right, the workload proves its identity to a token service and calls the cloud API with a token that expires in about fifteen minutes, so a leaked copy is soon useless.
diagrams.caption: The best secret is one that does not exist. Workload identity plus short-lived tokens removes the long-lived value an attacker would steal.

diagrams.title: A CI job gets cloud credentials with OIDC, no stored keys
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram. A CI job asks the CI platform's OIDC issuer for a signed identity token describing the repository and branch. It sends the token to the cloud's security token service, which fetches the issuer's public keys, verifies the token and checks the claims against the role's trust policy, then returns credentials that expire in about an hour. The job deploys with them.
diagrams.caption: No cloud secret is stored in CI. The trust policy decides which repository, branch or environment may assume the role, so a fork or another repo gets nothing.

messages.label: request ID token (aud=sts)
messages.note: The job must be allowed to mint tokens; in GitHub Actions that is `permissions: id-token: write`. The audience names the cloud service that will accept it.

messages.label: signed JWT: repo, ref, env
messages.note: Claims identify the workflow run: repository, branch or tag, environment. The token itself lives a few minutes.

messages.label: exchange JWT for role creds
messages.note: On AWS this is `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`; Azure and Google Cloud have equivalent federated-credential flows.

messages.label: fetch signing keys (cached)
messages.note: The cloud trusts the issuer's published keys, configured once as an identity provider.

messages.label: temp credentials (~1 h)
messages.note: Only after verifying signature, issuer and audience, and that the subject matches the trust policy, for example only `main` of one repository, or one protected environment.

messages.label: deploy with temp creds
messages.note: The credentials expire on their own. If the log leaks them, the window is short and scoped to one deploy role.

diagrams.title: Responding to a leaked key (illustrative)
diagrams.alt: Illustrative timeline of a leaked cloud key. At T plus 0 a developer pushes a key to a public repository. Within minutes automated scanners find it and unusual API calls begin. A secret-scanning alert fires, the team revokes the key, issues a replacement, reviews audit logs, and finally adds push protection and moves the service to workload identity.
diagrams.caption: Illustrative, not a real incident. Revoke first, then clean up: deleting the commit does not un-leak a key that bots already copied.

events.label: Key committed and pushed to a public repository
Automated scrapers find it; unusual API calls start from unknown IPs
Secret-scanning alert and a billing anomaly page the on-call engineer
Key revoked at the provider; a replacement issued through the vault
Audit logs reviewed for everything the key touched; attacker resources removed
Git history cleaned for hygiene only; the key is already dead
Push protection on, service moved to workload identity, no static key left

diagrams.title: A hardened build and release pipeline
diagrams.alt: Flow from reviewed source through an ephemeral build runner that installs pinned dependencies, to a signing step that produces a signature and provenance, to an artifact registry, to a deploy step that verifies the signature and provenance before running. A pull request from a fork reaches only a separate test job with read-only permissions and no secrets.
diagrams.caption: Every hop either reduces what an attacker can change or verifies it was not changed. Untrusted code never runs where secrets live.

steps.text: Changes reach the release branch only through review and branch protection. Builds start from an exact commit, not a moving branch name.

The build runs on a fresh runner, installs dependencies from the lockfile with hashes, uses CI actions and base images pinned by commit SHA or digest, and gets cloud access through OIDC, not stored keys.
The artifact is signed and a provenance statement records the source commit, builder and inputs (the idea behind SLSA). The registry addresses it by digest, so a tag cannot be swapped silently.
Deployment verifies the signature and checks that the provenance names the expected repository and builder before anything runs.
Pull requests from forks run in a separate job with a read-only token and no secrets. Do not combine privileged triggers such as `pull_request_target` with checking out and running the PR's code.

diagrams.title: Supply-chain controls: effort vs risk reduced
diagrams.alt: Chart of supply-chain controls by effort and risk reduced. Committing a lockfile and installing with it is low effort and fairly effective. Dependency alerts are low effort and moderate. Pinning CI actions by SHA is low effort and effective. An SBOM is moderate effort and mainly improves visibility. A private mirror is high effort and effective. Signature and provenance checks at deploy are the most effort and the most protection.
diagrams.caption: Rough positions, not measurements. Do the cheap, high-value controls first (lockfiles, pinning, alerts), then invest in mirrors and provenance for critical services.

examples.title: Fetch secrets at runtime with the workload's identity

bad.label: Database password committed with the code

good.label: Read from the secret manager using the pod's role

examples.why: The repository now holds only a name, and access is controlled by an IAM policy you can audit and revoke. Better still, where the database supports it, use identity-based database auth with short-lived tokens so there is no password at all.

examples.title: CI: federated identity, least privilege, pinned actions

bad.label: Static cloud keys, broad token, floating tags
bad.code:
on: [push, pull_request_target]
permissions: write-all
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_KEY }}
      AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { ref: "${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}" }
      - uses: some-org/deploy-action@main
      - run: ./deploy.sh

good.label: OIDC role, read-only by default, pinned by SHA
good.code:
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production          # protected: required reviewers
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write                # allow this job to request an OIDC token
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha>   # v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@<full-commit-sha>   # v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy-orders
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: ./deploy.sh

examples.why: The bad workflow runs a fork's code (via `pull_request_target` plus checking out the PR head) in a job that holds long-lived cloud keys and a write-all token, and pulls an action from a moving branch. The good one deploys only from `main`, has no stored cloud secret, scopes the token to read, and pins third-party code to an immutable commit (keep the version in a comment so update tools can bump it).

examples.title: Install exactly what was reviewed

bad.label: Resolve fresh versions on every build
bad.code:
npm install
pip install requests flask

good.label: Lockfile-only installs, hashes for Python
good.code:
npm ci                                   # fails if package-lock.json and package.json disagree
pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt   # every line pinned with ==version and --hash

examples.why: `npm install` and unpinned `pip install` can pull a new, possibly compromised release between your review and your build. Lockfile installs are reproducible, and hashes make the build fail if a registry serves different bytes for the same version. Dependency update bots then propose upgrades as reviewable diffs.

checklist: No secrets in source, images, tickets or chat; secret scanning with push protection is on for every repository.
Services authenticate with a workload identity and fetch secrets or short-lived tokens at runtime from a vault or secret manager.
Each credential is scoped to one service and the minimum actions; humans get just-in-time, audited access to production secrets.
Rotation is automated, supports two valid versions during the overlap, and has been rehearsed; revocation of any key takes minutes.
Dependencies are installed from a committed lockfile (with hashes where supported); internal package names are reserved or scoped to stop dependency confusion.
An SBOM is produced per release and vulnerability alerts are triaged against an agreed patch SLA.
CI tokens are read-only by default, cloud access uses OIDC federation, third-party actions and base images are pinned by SHA or digest.
Untrusted pull-request code never runs in a job with secrets; releases are signed and deployment verifies signature and provenance.

antipatterns.title: A long-lived key in the repository

bad.label: Key committed once, valid for months

better.label: Workload identity and short-lived credentials
better.code:
Pod / VM / CI job identity  ->  token service  ->  credentials valid for minutes, one role
Repository contains: role name, secret path. Never the value.

antipatterns.why: A long-lived key has no natural end, is copied into every clone, fork and backup, and usually has broader access than anyone remembers. Short-lived credentials make a leak a small, self-healing incident.

antipatterns.title: Deleting the commit instead of revoking the key

bad.label: Hide the evidence and hope
bad.code:
git rm .env && git commit -m "remove secrets"
git push --force

better.label: Revoke, replace, investigate, then clean up
better.code:
1. Revoke the key at the provider (now)
2. Issue a replacement through the vault; redeploy
3. Review audit logs for what the key did
4. Then rewrite history for hygiene and add push protection

antipatterns.why: Once pushed, assume the key has been copied: forks, caches, CI logs and automated scrapers all may have it. Only revocation removes the attacker's access.

antipatterns.title: One powerful CI credential shared by every pipeline

bad.label: Org-wide admin token available to all repos
bad.code:
# organisation secret, visible to every repository
CLOUD_ADMIN_KEY: <owner-level access to all accounts>

better.label: Per-repo, per-environment roles via OIDC
better.code:
role deploy-orders-prod  trusts: repo acme/orders, environment production
role deploy-web-staging  trusts: repo acme/web,    branch main
each role: only the services and regions it deploys

antipatterns.why: With one shared admin key, compromising any repository's pipeline, including a test job or a malicious dependency's install script, compromises everything. Narrow trust policies limit an incident to one service in one environment.

interview: Open with the principle: "I design assuming a secret will leak and a dependency will be compromised, so I limit lifetime, scope and blast radius."
Describe the runtime path concretely: workload identity, fetch from a secret manager or exchange for a short-lived token, keep it in memory, audit every read.
Explain rotation with overlap (two valid versions) and that revocation, not deleting the commit, is the first step after a leak.
For CI, mention OIDC federation instead of stored cloud keys, read-only default tokens, pinning by SHA, and keeping fork PR code away from secrets.
On dependencies, name concrete risks (typosquatting, dependency confusion, hijacked maintainer, install scripts) and concrete controls (lockfiles with hashes, mirror, SBOM, patch SLA).

At SSE level, frame it as an org-wide programme: paved-road templates, policy-as-code checks, a tested leaked-secret runbook, and incremental SLSA-style provenance for critical services. Be honest that signing proves origin, not safety.

quiz.question: A developer pushes an API key to a public repository and notices five minutes later. What should happen first?
choices: Force-push a commit that removes the key
Revoke the key at the provider and issue a replacement
Open a ticket to rotate it next sprint
quiz.explain: Assume it has already been copied; scrapers watch public pushes. Only revocation stops abuse. Then replace it, review audit logs for what it was used for, and clean the history afterwards.

quiz.question: What does OIDC federation from CI to a cloud provider remove?
choices: The need for any access policy
Long-lived cloud keys stored as CI secrets
quiz.explain: The CI job proves its identity with a short-lived signed token and exchanges it for temporary credentials. The trust policy limits which repo, branch or environment can assume the role, and nothing long-lived is stored.

quiz.question: Your company uses an internal package `acme-utils`. Someone publishes `acme-utils` 99.0.0 to the public registry and a build picks it up. What is this attack called?
quiz.explain: The resolver preferred the higher public version over the private one. Use a scoped namespace or reserved names, point installs at one registry or mirror that proxies public packages, and install from a lockfile.

quiz.question: Why pin a third-party CI action to a full commit SHA instead of `@v4`?
choices: A tag can be moved to point at different code; a commit SHA cannot
Tags are not supported in workflows
quiz.explain: If the action's repository is compromised, an attacker can retag `v4` to malicious code and every workflow using the tag runs it. A full SHA is immutable. Keep the version in a comment so update bots can propose bumps.

quiz.question: What does a valid Sigstore signature with SLSA provenance on an artifact tell you?
choices: Who built it, from which source and on which builder, and that it was not altered since
That the dependency is free of malware
quiz.explain: Signatures and provenance establish origin and integrity: this artifact came from that repo and build platform and was not modified. They say nothing about whether the source itself is safe, which still needs review and scanning.

practice.prompt: You join a company where services read database passwords and cloud keys from environment files baked into container images, and every CI pipeline uses one shared cloud admin key. Lay out a plan to fix secrets and supply-chain risk over the next two quarters.
practice.answer: First contain: turn on secret scanning with push protection across all repositories, inventory existing secrets (scan images and history), and rotate anything exposed, starting with the shared CI admin key. Replace that key with OIDC federation: one cloud role per repository and environment, with a trust policy pinned to repo and branch or protected environment, and least-privilege permissions. Default CI tokens to read-only, pin actions by SHA, and move fork PR builds to jobs without secrets. For services, adopt a secret manager or vault: workloads authenticate with their pod or instance identity, fetch secrets at startup, and where possible switch to identity-based database auth with short-lived tokens. Remove env files from images and rebuild. Automate rotation with two valid versions during an overlap window, and write and rehearse a leaked-secret runbook (revoke, replace, review audit logs, clean up). For dependencies: enforce lockfile installs (`npm ci`, hash-pinned Python requirements), route installs through an internal mirror with reserved internal names, generate an SBOM per release, and agree a patch SLA for critical vulnerabilities. For critical services, sign images and generate build provenance, and have deployment verify them. Measure progress: number of static keys left, rotation age, mean time to revoke, percentage of repos on the paved road.
rubric: Contains first: scanning, inventory, and rotating the shared admin key immediately
Replaces stored cloud keys with OIDC federation and narrowly scoped per-repo roles
Moves services to runtime secret fetching or identity-based short-lived credentials, with automated rotation and overlap
Hardens CI: read-only defaults, pinned actions, no secrets for untrusted PR code
Covers dependency controls: lockfiles with hashes, mirror, dependency confusion, SBOM, patch SLA
Describes signing and provenance accurately (origin and integrity, not safety) and defines measurable progress
